text:
Parliament has cleared the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026, which changes a law on the rights of transgender persons enacted in 2019. The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in mid-March 2026 by Social Justice Minister Virendra Kumar, whose ministry administers the 2019 law. Its central change is to omit the provision that gives transgender persons the right to self-perceived gender identity. That right rests on a landmark Supreme Court judgment, which held that gender identity could be recognised without sex reassignment surgery and also recognised a third gender category.

The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 24 March 2026 by voice vote, amid a walkout by the Opposition. Replying to the debate, Virendra Kumar said the legislation was meant to protect people facing discrimination on the basis of biological factors. The amended law routes recognition through certification by a medical board.

The Bill also introduces graded punishments for offences against transgender persons. Forcing a person into a transgender identity, or compelling a person to beg or work in servitude, attracts heavier penalties under the amended text, with higher penalties where the victim is a child. Critics said the medical boards would add bureaucratic hurdles for people seeking recognition.

The Rajya Sabha took up the Bill the next day. On 25 March 2026, the Upper House passed it. Opposition members alleged that the Bill excluded gay and lesbian persons, and argued that it went against the Supreme Court's earlier ruling on self-identification. The government maintained that the changes were needed to protect people on the basis of biological and physiological characteristics.

President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent to the Bill on 30 March 2026, and it became the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026. The 2019 Act had been passed by Parliament to give statutory form to the rights recognised by the Supreme Court. Reports on the amended law say it narrows the definition of transgender persons to those with certain biological or physiological characteristics, intersex variations, or socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta, and makes medical certification a requirement for recognition. Opponents said the changes reduce the protection that transgender persons had enjoyed under the 2019 law.

Under the 2019 Act, a person applied to the District Magistrate for a certificate, and that certificate conferred the right to self-perceived gender identity. The 2026 amendment changes that route. The Opposition, including the Congress, described the Bill as an unconstitutional regression, and some members argued that the Bill left sexual orientation out of its scope.

questions.q: The landmark Supreme Court judgment that recognised the right to self-perceived gender identity was delivered in which year?
questions.explanation: The NALSA judgment, which upheld self-perceived gender identity and recognised a third gender, was delivered in 2014. The 2019 Act was enacted to build on it. The passage does not give the year.

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution of India does the President give or withhold assent to a Bill passed by Parliament?
questions.explanation: Article 111 deals with assent to Bills: the President must either give assent or withhold it, and a non-Money Bill may be returned once for reconsideration. Article 110 defines Money Bills.

list2: A. Procedure for amending the Constitution
B. Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights
D. Protection of life and personal liberty
questions.explanation: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; Article 32 lets a person move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights; Article 111 covers assent to Bills; Article 368 sets the amendment procedure.

statements: I. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 came into force on 10 January 2020.
II. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 was passed by Parliament in 2020.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true: the Act came into force on 10 January 2020 by notification S.O. 135(E). Statement II is false: Parliament passed the Act in 2019, and it received presidential assent on 5 December 2019.

statements: 1. A Bill to amend the Constitution must be passed in each House by a majority of its total membership and by a majority of at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.
2. Under Article 111, the President may return a Bill other than a Money Bill to the Houses for reconsideration.
3. Under Article 32, only the High Courts can issue writs to enforce fundamental rights.
4. The President may withhold assent to a constitutional amendment Bill that has been passed by both Houses with the required majority.
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct (Article 368(2) and the Article 111 proviso). Statement 3 is wrong because Article 32 is a Supreme Court power, while High Courts have writ power under Article 226. Statement 4 is wrong because Article 368(2) says the President shall give assent. Two statements are incorrect.

title: Transgender Rights Amendment Bill
